events.text:
The U.S. Navy has publicly disclosed a previously unannounced AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile (LRAAM), also known as the "Malice", revealing the weapon mounted inside the internal weapons bay of an F-35C Lightning II with an AIM-120 AMRAAM mounted on the bay door. The Navy describes the AIM-424 as its next-generation, long range air to air missile, intended to give Navy and Marine Corps aviators greater capability against advanced threats.
The internal carriage is particularly significant. Rather than simply adding another externally carried long-range missile, the AIM-424 appears to have been designed around the F-35's limited internal weapons-bay dimensions, allowing the aircraft to retain its low-observable configuration while carrying a substantially longer-range air-to-air weapon.
The missile is still associated with testing and development, and the Navy has released few technical details regarding its range, seeker, propulsion or intended employment. The available imagery does, however, show the AIM-424 being evaluated on both the F-35C and F/A-18E/F, indicating that the weapon is being considered across the Navy's carrier aviation force.
Source: https://www.dvidshub.net/image/9879420/aim-424-long-range-air-air-missile-lraam

👁 How Pokemon-chasing children were fooled into building Pentagon's next-gen drone eye
For nine years, Pokemon Go urged children and parents to go outside with their cameras to hunt down virtual creatures through the real world.
Scanning streets and parks in seemingly harmless fun, the players were in reality data mining – unwittingly building up a vast dataset, per Dutch daily Trouw.
➡️ Roughly 30 billion scans were handed over to US software development company and the video game developer Niantic, allowing it to quietly build a 3D model of the physical world
➡️ Players surrendered street-level scans of public and private spaces, interior footage of homes, and biometric-adjacent information from camera angles
➡️ The game's terms gave Niantic a transferable, sublicensable license for submitted content - every scan could be resold and repurposed without further consent
➡️ These scans helped train Niantic’s Visual Positioning System (VPS)
➡️ Where GPS fails, VPS matches what a camera sees against a 3D model of the world, and two recognizable reference points can fix a position – well-suited for autonomous drones operating beyond satellite reach
The corporate lineage fits the playbook:
♦️ Niantic founder John Hanke served in the US Foreign Service before co-founding Keyhole, named after America’s KH spy satellites
♦️ When it neared collapse, In-Q-Tel - the CIA’s venture arm - and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency money kept it alive so the tech could “support United States troops in Iraq”
♦️ Google bought Keyhole, turned it into Google Earth, and spun Niantic out in 2015 - Pokemon Go arrived a year later
♦️ In 2025, the company split: the game part was sold to Scopely (Saudi-backed) for $3.5 billion while the mapping tech stayed with Niantic Spatial
♦️ That tech then partnered with Vantor - the rebranded Maxar Intelligence, a major NGA contractor serving defense and intelligence clients
♦️ Vantor is the US[ intel engine](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71518) behind Volodymyr Zelensky’s drone campaign against Russia
♦️ The Niantic Spatial - Vantor partnership plans to combine Niantic's ground-based Visual Positioning System with Vantor's aerial positioning software, allowing air and ground systems to share coordinates without satellite signals
Now that technology is being polished, packaged, and handed to Pentagon-linked partners so drones can keep flying when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or simply nonexistent.
The companies insist no raw game data ever takes flight on drones. But once that training data is distilled into patterns, the original contributions become impossible to trace - or claw back.

These private-sector employees are to embed within the State Department for one-year stints unpaid by the agency, reports Foreign Policy. 
The State Department expects the first participant to begin work “within the year,” according to an unnamed State Department spokesperson.

🔴 The Trump administration’s hollow defense has been to claim that these partners were selected “based on expertise in digital freedom-related areas that are critical to our national security,” and that they understand the "cost of censorship."

🇺🇸🛢US Hormuz operation: a secret corridor that exposes American weakness
 
The US military has been running a covert operation for the past several weeks to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz, with tankers transiting each night along a southern channel off the Omani coast, according to Axios.
The current volume is roughly half the pre-war export level, and the number of tankers is five times lower, yet US officials have presented it as evidence of control over the waterway.
The narrative of control, however, is at odds with the reality of the operation.
🔴 The US is moving oil at night, in a southern channel, at maximum distance from Iranian drones and missiles, and only during limited time windows
🔴 Several ships have been hit by Iranian attacks after violating passage rules, and most commercial operators are unwilling to undertake such transits without Iranian coordination
🔴 The Strait remains open to shipping from the Iranian side. Iran has allowed tankers bound for China, Russia, Pakistan, and Iraq to pass through, undermining US claims about saving the global economy
👉 While US officials tout the Hormuz operation as a success, the direct military cost of the war has already exceeded $42 billion. The gasoline prices in the US are up roughly 45% compared to pre-war levels, with the national average remaining above $4.10 per gallon throughout August. The administration's pivot to economic warfare against Iran has created a paradox: tighter sanctions mean tighter global supplies, and higher costs for American households.
Analysts say the current operation is only a short-term workaround that allows Trump to claim greater control over the Strait. While it has mitigated some economic disruption, the broader conflict remains unresolved, and the US is still forced to move oil like a smuggler, not a power that controls the waterway.
